cues.text: A Host Taken in a Raid
On June 24, 1300, amid military plundering near the village of Niervaart , close to Breda in the southern Netherlands, a soldier stole a consecrated Host from a local church.

The surviving accounts do not agree on whose forces were responsible, and this entry does not repeat more specific claims found in devotional retellings that cannot be independently confirmed for this date.
Found Beneath a Clump of Dirt
Not long afterward, a farmer named Jan Bautoen was working a plot of land near Niervaart when he came upon the Host again.
It was hidden beneath a clump of dirt where it had apparently been discarded or lost.
By every surviving account, it was found in perfect condition, its form entirely unspoiled by the time it had spent exposed to the open ground.
One of the most complete surviving accounts of the episode comes from an investigation conducted by the Bishop of Liège.
His inquiry into the matter helped establish the tradition's early credibility.
The relic was placed in a precious container and, according to the tradition, the species of bread remained visibly intact for a considerable time afterward.
A Church That Preserved the Memory
Traces of the miracle survive in church documents and devotional paintings created to commemorate the event.
These form part of a broader Dutch tradition of Eucharistic devotion that would, in the following century, also produce the accounts venerated at Amsterdam, Boxtel, and Meerssen.
The Miracle of Breda-Niervaart remains counted among the oldest of the Netherlands' documented Eucharistic traditions.
It is a modest account — no fire, no desecration, simply a theft undone and a relic recovered whole — that nonetheless anchors a devotional history.
The Low Countries would go on to build that history considerably further in the centuries that followed.
